In addition, as the agent for the Bahamas has already discussed, the proportional allocation of mitigation duties must reflect the principle of common but differentiated responsibility, which is well recognized in international law. But CBDR does not eclipse proportionality rule itself. It rather informs our assessment of what legal burden a state can reasonably bear, given its developmental capacity. That is all that I wish to say today on the prevention obligation. I now want to turn briefly to the role of the climate treaties. They also impose individual obligations on states to mitigate. And unsurprisingly, such obligations are consistent with the state's obligations under customary international law. I will touch upon two obligations under the Paris Agreement. First, Article 4.2 of the Paris Agreement requires states to prepare, communicate, and maintain successive nationally determined contributions, or NDCs. These NDCs are not an aspirational wish list, or a purely discretionary decision, or an unguided exercise. Their setting is a matter of concrete, binding obligations. Let us go back to first principle. Treaty obligations must be interpreted in light of the treaty's object and purpose. In the Paris Agreement, that is expressly stated in Article 2A. That is, to limit the increase in global average temperatures to well below 2 degrees above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 degrees. The Paris Agreement, like all other treaties, must also be performed in good faith. So while states are not obliged to achieve the temperature goal, they are required to set their NDCs in a way that makes it possible to achieve the aim. To that end, NDCs must reflect a state's highest possible ambition and represent a progression over time and be informed by the decisions of the Conference of Parties and the outcomes of the global stocktake. Just a brief note here on the global stocktake, because the Paris Agreement expressly requires states to take it into account in their NDCs. The 2023 stocktake makes clear that states are not on track to achieve the temperature goal. States must therefore urgently take steps to set and meet NDCs that can, in fact, result in deep, rapid and sustained reduction in global emissions in line with the 1.5 degree goal. That is what good faith requires. States obligations under the Paris Agreement do not, however, end there. Article 4.2 also requires that states pursue domestic mitigation measures with a view to meeting their NDCs. This is not an obligation to actually meet the NDCs in all circumstances, but it requires that states act with diligence and pursue domestic policies which are reasonably aligned with their NDCs. One critical tool in the state's arsenal is the regulation of private actors who generate a considerable portion of greenhouse gas emissions. and I refer the Court to the Bahamas' written submissions, which discusses this obligation in more detail. In sum, States must diligently pursue mitigation measures in line with their NDCs, which in turn must reflect States' progress or indeed their lack of progress towards the temperature goal. There is no other way of interpreting the Paris agreement without doing grave violence to the fundamental principles of treaty interpretation or international law. At this juncture, it is worth noting that other rules of international law also give rise to mitigation obligations. Those include the law of the sea and human rights, both of which enshrine binding norms on the protection of the environment. Earlier this year, ITLOS affirmed states' obligations to prevent and reduce marine pollution in the form of greenhouse gas emissions. In the human rights sphere, there is no shortage of judicial decisions affirming states' obligations under international law. I commend those decisions to the Court and refer the Court also to the Bahamas' written submissions on these matters. Mr. President, Excellencies, before I conclude, there is one final point that I will mention briefly, and that is the interrelation of the various bodies of law that are applicable to climate change. They did not erase existing public international law. and those who claim otherwise provide no credible support for their proposition. The court should resist such harmful attempts to dilute and distort international law. Mr. President, honourable members of the court, you have the heavy burden of carrying out the court's mission of upholding international law. On behalf of the Bahamas and the present and future generations of people who share this planet, I implore you to be bold as you pen and deliver your opinion. It has been an honour to appear before you, and I thank you for your kind attention.

Mr. President, distinguished members of the court, I'm honored to appear in this historic proceeding on behalf of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. I will be addressing the harmonization of the multiple regimes of international law referred to in the first question before the court. These different branches of international law are all from the same tree, and they all lead to a single overriding obligation, namely that all states must take the necessary measures to deeply and rapidly mitigate anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions to avoid breaching the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold, with the greatest burden falling on the developed and high-emitting states. As recognised in the reports of the IPCC and the Paris agreement, holding the increase in global temperature to 1.5 degrees Celsius would significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change. This pivotal obligation arises from distinct but interrelated and mutually reinforcing legal regimes, including principles of customary international law on transboundary harm to the environment, the UN climate change regime, comprised primarily of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, and fundamental norms of international human rights law, including the right to development. All are to be applied in conjunction with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. I will speak to each in turn. First, as the Court recognized in Pulp Mills, under customary international law, each state is under a core obligation to use all means at its disposal to prevent activities taking place in its territory that cause significant damage to the environment of another state. There is no doubt that greenhouse gas emissions cause significant, indeed catastrophic, transboundary harm. Their long-term and global impact in no way diminishes application of this fundamental principle. Moreover, as confirmed in the unanimous ILOS advisory opinion on climate change, a stringent standard of due diligence applies in preventing harm to the marine environment. The core obligations under UNCLOS part XII reflect customary international law. There is no reason why a less exacting standard should apply to the environment as a whole. Second, While the UN climate change regime is critical to mitigation, it is not the last word on states' obligations. The obligations under those treaties are largely procedural. They simply require states to formulate and communicate nationally determined contributions, reflecting their highest possible ambition, and to ensure that successive contributions represent a progression of efforts over time. Some have argued in these proceedings that this specialized regime is somehow self-contained or even lex specialis, with the consequence that international law cannot impose obligations that go beyond the Paris Agreement. That position is manifestly inconsistent with the strong presumption against normative conflict and fragmentation. As the Court noted in the Rite of Passage over Indian Territory case, treaties should be interpreted as producing and as intended to produce effects in accordance with existing law and not in violation of it. It cannot be that the Paris agreement is intended to violate pre-existing obligations to protect the environment. It is notable that in 1993, the court had created a chamber for environmental matters. It was discontinued in 2006 because, as President Higgins explained at the time, states understandably saw environmental law as part of international law as a whole. It cannot be that the intention of the Paris Agreement is to protect the planetary climate system by excluding international law as a whole, not least when our common survival is at stake. In the words of the ILC report on fragmentation, without the principle of systemic integration, it would be impossible to give expression to and keep alive any sense of the common good of humankind. Bangladesh notes further that for lex specialis to apply, there must be some actual inconsistency between norms. But there is no such conflict between the Paris Agreement and general international law. Simply put, the lex specialis argument is missing the lex. It was squarely rejected by ITLOS, and it should similarly be rejected by this Court. Invoking the Paris agreement to avoid pre-existing obligations is particularly troubling, because the earth has already reached a year-long temperature exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius. There is obviously a substantial emissions gap. It cannot be that grossly inadequate NDCs somehow satisfy the obligation to protect the environment. It is high time for the faltering COP process to be reinvigorated by a robust opinion from this Court. The time for empty promises has passed. I now turn to the third point, namely that climate change poses an immediate, if not the greatest, threat to human rights. This implicates the inter-State dimension of human rights obligations, including article 2 of the Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, requiring States parties to take steps individually and through international assistance and cooperation especially economic and technical, to achieve progressively the full realization of rights. It is reinforced by the UN Declaration on the Right to Development, recognizing the duty of cooperation in ensuring development and eliminating obstacles to development. At a minimum, States must not impede another State's ability to protect and ensure the rights of its population. The fourth point is that these norms must be applied in conjunction with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. This requires developed States to mitigate emissions consistent with their greater financial and technical capabilities, even if all States must make mitigation efforts. This is a fundamental aspect of the equity that international law requires. I return to where I started. Each of these legal regimes leads to one overarching obligation, to mitigate emissions to avoid breaching the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold. That is the key obligation, as it is the only way to prevent the catastrophic harms that are predicted by the IPCC in a 2 degrees or 3 degrees Celsius scenario. However, that is not enough. Mr. President, distinguished members of the court, behind the abstract legal questions that are before you, beyond the walls of this great hall of justice, is a world of immense suffering. As multiple states acknowledge, adaptation-related obligations are primary obligations. They are not alternatives to mitigation. but are required in parallel, and in some circumstances, the same measures may be required in relation to both. At the same time, adaptation measures are also secondary obligations that can arise when states violate their obligations to mitigate GHG emissions in line with the best available science. As such, states' adaptation-related obligations are preventive and responsive in nature and relevant to both questions A and B. Turning to my second point, the same legal framework underpins states' mitigation and adaptation obligations. This includes the core obligation under customary international environmental law to prevent and reduce significant transboundary harms related to GHG emissions. the duty of due diligence measured on an objective and stringent basis, the duty to cooperate to, quote, "jointly manage the risks of damage to the environment," territorial sovereignty and self-determination, international human rights obligations, and express requirements in respect of adaptation under the UN climate change regime and UNCLOS. As in the mitigation context, adaptation obligations are informed by the best available science and subject to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Accordingly, state-specific adaptation obligations will be based on their technical and financial capabilities and their historical contributions to climate change. At least four specific concrete obligations in respect of adaptation flow from this normative framework. First, developed states must take affirmative measures to ensure that the funds necessary to adapt to climate impacts are available and accessible. The IPCC has concluded that, quote, "Gaps exist between current levels of adaptation and levels needed to respond to impacts and reduce climate risks," end quote, and that at current rates of planning and implementation, these gaps will continue to grow. Article 4.4 of the UNFCCC provides that developed states, quote, "shall also assist," end quote, developing states, end quote, "meeting costs of adaptation," end quote. The Paris Agreement is likewise not aspirational. Under Article 7.9, for example, all states, quote, "shall, as appropriate, engage in adaptation planning processes and the implementation of," end quote, adaptation actions. Article 9.1 demands that developed states, quote, "shall provide financial resources to assist developing country parties with respect to both mitigation and adaptation."
